name: Grandpa
text:
Come closer, and I'll tell you why I still make boats out of orange peel. I was eleven that summer. My little sister, Ana, had never seen the sea. Neither had I, but being the older one, I pretended I knew all about it.

Behind our house there was an irrigation channel. Most days it was barely deep enough to wet your shoes. To Ana it was a river, and I told her every river eventually found the sea. She asked how long it would take us to sail there. That was the trouble with Ana. She believed my explanations and then expected me to do something about them.

Our father had brought home three oranges from the market. They were a treat, so we ate them slowly. I peeled mine in one long strip, curled it into a little boat, and pushed a twig through the middle for a mast. Ana tore a corner from an old flour sack for the sail. She wanted a passenger. We chose the smallest button from Mother's sewing tin. I told her it was a captain, and she named him Captain Button.

We launched him after lunch. The boat caught in the weeds. Ana freed it with a stick. Then it stuck under a stone, and I got both my shoes wet helping it out. We followed it past the fig tree, past the washhouse, all the way to the little bridge. At every bend Ana shouted that the sea must be just around the next corner.

Then the rain came. Not a little shower. One of those summer storms that makes the whole sky seem to fall into the road. The channel rose so quickly that our boat disappeared under the bridge before we could reach it. Ana started after it. I caught her hand and pulled her back. She was furious. Then she cried, and I felt worse than I ever had in my eleven important years.

We sheltered in the washhouse until Father found us. I expected a terrible scolding. He wrapped his coat around Ana and asked me what had happened. I told him about the boat, the captain, and my promise to get her to the sea. He was quiet for a while. Then he said, 'You brought your sister home. That was the important voyage.' I didn't understand how he could call a journey successful when we had lost the boat.

The next morning Ana was waiting by my bed. In her hand was Captain Button. She had rescued him when the boat caught under the stone, before the storm, and kept him safe in her pocket. She had forgotten to tell me. We laughed so much that Mother came to see what was wrong.

We never found the orange-peel boat. But we made another. And another. Years later, when I finally took Ana to the real sea, she brought that button. She held it up to the water and told him he'd arrived. So when you see me peeling an orange very carefully, now you know. I'm not trying to make a perfect peel. I'm remembering a captain, my sister, and the first voyage that taught me what it means to bring someone home.
dedication: For the next little adventurers in our family
